work.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
          <jats:sec>
            <jats:title/>
            <jats:p>
              We developed a nondestructive three-dimensional microbial visualization method utilizing synchrotron radiation X-ray microscale computed tomography to better understand the relationship between microorganisms and their surrounding habitats. The method was tested and optimized using a mixture of axenic
              <jats:italic>Escherichia coli</jats:italic>
              and
              <jats:italic>Comamonas testosteroni</jats:italic>
              . The osmium-thiocarbohydrazide-osmium method was used to stain all the microbial cells, and gold
              <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
              hybridization was used to detect specific phylogenetic microbial groups. The stained samples were embedded in epoxy resin for microtomographic analysis. Differences in X-ray absorbances were calculated by subtracting the pre-L
              <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
              -edge images from the post-L
              <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
              -edge images to visualize the osmium and gold signals. Although we successfully detected cells stained with osmium, those labeled with gold were not detected, probably because of the insufficient density of gold atoms in the microbial cells. We then applied the developed technique to anaerobic granules and visualized the distribution of microbial cells and extracellular polymeric substances. Empty spaces were highlighted to determine the cavity distribution in granules. Numerous independent cavities of different sizes were identified in the granules. The developed method can be applied to various environmental samples for deeper insights into microbial life in their habitats.
            </jats:p>
          </jats:sec>
          <jats:sec>
            <jats:title>IMPORTANCE</jats:title>
            <jats:p>
              Microorganisms inhabit diverse environments and often form biofilms. One factor that affects their community structure is the surrounding physical environment. The arrangement of residential space within the formed biofilm plays a crucial role in the supply and transportation of substances, as well as the discharge of metabolites. Conventional approaches, such as scanning electron microscopy and confocal laser scanning microscopy combined with fluorescence in
              <jats:italic>situ</jats:italic>
              hybridization, have limitations as they provide information primarily from the biofilm surface and cross-sections. In this study, we developed a method for detecting microorganisms in biofilms using synchrotron radiation X-ray microscale computer tomography. The developed method allows nondestructive three-dimensional observation of biofilms at a single-cell resolution (voxel size of approximately 200 nm), facilitating an understanding of the relationship between microorganisms and their physical habitats.
            </jats:p>
          </jats:sec>
title: Nondestructive and three-dimensional visualization by identifying elements using synchrotron radiation microscale X-ray CT reveals microbial and cavity distributions in anaerobic granular sludge

work.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
          <jats:p>
            The microbial community structure and spatial distribution of microorganisms and their in situ activities in anaerobic granules were investigated by 16S rRNA gene-based molecular techniques and microsensors for CH
            <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
            , H
            <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
            , pH, and the oxidation-reduction potential (ORP). The 16S rRNA gene-cloning analysis revealed that the clones related to the phyla
            <jats:italic>Alphaproteobacteria</jats:italic>
            (detection frequency, 51%),
            <jats:italic>Firmicutes</jats:italic>
            (20%),
            <jats:italic>Chloroflexi</jats:italic>
            (9%), and
            <jats:italic>Betaproteobacteria</jats:italic>
            (8%) dominated the bacterial clone library, and the predominant clones in the archaeal clone library were affiliated with
            <jats:italic>Methanosaeta</jats:italic>
            (73%). In situ hybridization with oligonucleotide probes at the phylum level revealed that these microorganisms were numerically abundant in the granule. A layered structure of microorganisms was found in the granule, where
            <jats:italic>Chloroflexi</jats:italic>
            and
            <jats:italic>Betaproteobacteria</jats:italic>
            were present in the outer shell of the granule,
            <jats:italic>Firmicutes</jats:italic>
            were found in the middle layer, and aceticlastic
            <jats:italic>Archaea</jats:italic>
            were restricted to the inner layer. Microsensor measurements for CH
            <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
            , H
            <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
            , pH, and ORP revealed that acid and H
            <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
            production occurred in the upper part of the granule, below which H
            <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
            consumption and CH
            <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
            production were detected. Direct comparison of the in situ activity distribution with the spatial distribution of the microorganisms implied that
            <jats:italic>Chloroflexi</jats:italic>
            contributed to the degradation of complex organic compounds in the outermost layer, H
            <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
            was produced mainly by
            <jats:italic>Firmicutes</jats:italic>
            in the middle layer, and
            <jats:italic>Methanosaeta</jats:italic>
            produced CH
            <jats:sub>4</jats:sub>
            in the inner layer. We determined the effective diffusion coefficient for H
            <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
            in the anaerobic granules to be 2.66 × 10
            <jats:sup>−5</jats:sup>
            cm
            <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
            s
            <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
            , which was 57% in water.
          </jats:p>
title: Layered Structure of Bacterial and Archaeal Communities and Their In Situ Activities in Anaerobic Granules

work.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Dynamic reaction diffusion models were used to analyze the consequences of aggregation for syntrophic reactions in methanogenic ecosystems. Flocs from a whey digestor were used to measure all model parameters under the <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic> conditions of a particular defined biological system. Fermentation simulations without adjustable parameters could precisely predict the kinetics of H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> gas production of digestor flocs during syntrophic methanogenesis from ethanol. The results demonstrated a kinetic compartmentalization of H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> metabolism inside the flocs. The interspecies electron transfer reaction was mildly diffusion controlled. The H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> gas profiles across the flocs showed high H <jats:sub>2</jats:sub> concentrations inside the flocs at any time. Simulations of the syntrophic metabolism at low substrate concentrations such as in digestors or sediments showed that it is impossible to achieve high H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> gas turnovers at simultaneously low steady‐state H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> concentrations. This showed a mechanistic contradiction in the concept of postulated low H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> microenvironments for the anaerobic digestion process. The results of the computer experiments support the conclusion that syntrophic H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> production may only be a side reaction of H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> independent interspecies electron transfer in methanogenic ecosystems.</jats:p>
